light-year: The distance light travels in one year, about 9.46 trillion kilometers (5.88 trillion miles).
astronomical unit: The average distance between Earth and the Sun, about 150 million kilometers (93 million miles).
parsec: A distance unit used in astronomy equal to about 3.26 light-years.
exoplanet: A planet that orbits a star other than our Sun.
dwarf planet: A body like Pluto that orbits the Sun and is round, but hasn't cleared other objects from its orbital path.
black hole: A region where gravity is so strong that nothing, not even light, can escape.
supermassive black hole: A black hole millions to billions of times the Sun's mass, found at the center of most large galaxies.
event horizon: The boundary around a black hole beyond which nothing can escape.
Schwarzschild radius: The radius of a black hole's event horizon for a given mass.
spaghettification: The stretching of an object into a long thin shape by extreme tidal forces near a black hole.
neutron star: The ultra-dense collapsed core of a massive star, packing more than the Sun's mass into a city-sized sphere.
pulsar: A rapidly spinning neutron star that sweeps beams of radiation across space like a lighthouse.
magnetar: A neutron star with an extraordinarily powerful magnetic field.
quasar: An extremely bright galactic core powered by gas falling into a supermassive black hole.
white dwarf: The hot, dense, Earth-sized remnant left after a Sun-like star sheds its outer layers.
brown dwarf: An object too massive to be a planet but too small to sustain hydrogen fusion like a star.
red giant: A late-stage star that has swelled to a huge size and cooled after exhausting hydrogen in its core.
main sequence: The long, stable phase of a star's life when it fuses hydrogen into helium in its core.
Chandrasekhar limit: The maximum mass a white dwarf can have (about 1.4 solar masses) before collapsing.
supernova: The explosive death of a star, briefly outshining an entire galaxy.
nebula: A cloud of gas and dust in space, often where new stars form or the remains of a dead star.
nucleosynthesis: The creation of new atomic nuclei by nuclear fusion in stars or in the early universe.
protoplanetary disk: A rotating disk of gas and dust around a young star, from which planets form.
accretion disk: A swirling disk of matter spiraling onto a massive object such as a star or black hole.
globular cluster: A tightly bound, roughly spherical group of hundreds of thousands of old stars.
galaxy cluster: A group of hundreds to thousands of galaxies bound together by gravity.
Milky Way: The barred spiral galaxy containing our Solar System and hundreds of billions of stars.
Andromeda Galaxy: The nearest large spiral galaxy to the Milky Way, about 2.5 million light-years away.
dark matter: Invisible matter that doesn't emit light but whose gravity holds galaxies and clusters together.
dark energy: The unknown form of energy thought to be driving the accelerating expansion of the universe.
Big Bang: The theory that the universe began about 13.8 billion years ago from an extremely hot, dense state and has expanded since.
cosmic microwave background: Faint microwave radiation filling the universe, the leftover glow from about 380,000 years after the Big Bang.
CMB: Cosmic Microwave Background: the leftover radiation from the early universe, seen in every direction.
Hubble constant: The rate at which the universe is expanding, relating a galaxy's distance to how fast it recedes.
redshift: The stretching of light toward longer, redder wavelengths as an object moves away or space expands.
blueshift: The shift of light toward shorter, bluer wavelengths as an object moves toward the observer.
gravitational lensing: The bending of light from a distant object by the gravity of a massive object in between.
gravitational waves: Ripples in spacetime produced by accelerating masses, such as merging black holes.
spectroscopy: Splitting light into its wavelengths to learn an object's composition, temperature, and motion.
interferometry: Combining signals from multiple telescopes to achieve the resolution of a much larger one.
apparent magnitude: How bright a celestial object looks from Earth; lower numbers mean brighter.
absolute magnitude: How bright an object would appear from a standard distance of 10 parsecs, measuring its true luminosity.
albedo: The fraction of incoming light a surface reflects, from 0 (perfectly dark) to 1 (perfectly reflective).
light curve: A graph of an object's brightness over time, used to detect variable stars and exoplanet transits.
transit method: Detecting exoplanets by measuring the slight dimming of a star as a planet passes in front of it.
radial velocity: An object's speed toward or away from us; star wobbles in it reveal orbiting planets.
right ascension: The sky's equivalent of longitude, measured eastward along the celestial equator.
declination: The sky's equivalent of latitude, measured in degrees north or south of the celestial equator.
ecliptic: The apparent path the Sun traces across the sky over a year, marking the plane of Earth's orbit.
equinox: One of two moments each year when the Sun crosses the celestial equator and day and night are nearly equal.
solstice: One of two moments each year when the Sun reaches its farthest north or south point, giving the longest or shortest day.
perihelion: The point in an orbit where an object is closest to the Sun.
aphelion: The point in an orbit where an object is farthest from the Sun.
syzygy: The straight-line alignment of three celestial bodies, such as the Sun, Earth, and Moon during an eclipse.
solar eclipse: When the Moon passes between Earth and the Sun, blocking some or all of the Sun's light.
lunar eclipse: When Earth passes between the Sun and Moon, casting its shadow on the Moon.
tidal locking: When a body's rotation matches its orbit so the same side always faces its partner, as the Moon does with Earth.
Roche limit: The closest distance a moon can orbit a planet before tidal forces tear it apart.
Lagrange point: A spot where the gravity of two large bodies balances so a small object can stay in place relative to them.
escape velocity: The minimum speed needed to break free of a body's gravity without further propulsion.
geostationary orbit: An orbit about 35,786 km above the equator where a satellite keeps pace with Earth's rotation and appears fixed in the sky.
low Earth orbit: Orbits within about 2,000 km of Earth's surface, home to the International Space Station and most satellites.
Kuiper Belt: A region of icy bodies, including Pluto, beyond Neptune's orbit.
Oort Cloud: A theorized distant shell of icy objects surrounding the Solar System, thought to be the source of long-period comets.
asteroid belt: The region between Mars and Jupiter where most of the Solar System's asteroids orbit.
meteorite: A piece of rock or metal from space that survives its fall through the atmosphere and lands on the ground.
habitable zone: The range of distances from a star where a planet could have liquid water on its surface.
solar wind: A stream of charged particles flowing outward from the Sun.
coronal mass ejection: A huge burst of plasma and magnetic field from the Sun's corona that can trigger geomagnetic storms.
sunspot: A temporary dark, cooler patch on the Sun's surface caused by intense magnetic activity.
cosmic rays: High-energy particles from space, mostly protons, that strike Earth's atmosphere.
JWST: James Webb Space Telescope: NASA's infrared space observatory, launched in 2021, that studies the early universe and exoplanets.
James Webb Space Telescope: NASA's infrared space observatory, launched in 2021, that studies the early universe and exoplanets.
